Viết lại mỗi câu dưới đây dùng TỪ GỢI Ý (in hoa), giữ nguyên nghĩa và đúng dạng/collocation.
1. Many young professionals value owning branded possessions far more than they value experiences or relationships. (MATERIALISM)
2. Buying an expensive watch just to show colleagues how successful you are is a very obvious example of this kind of spending. (CONSPICUOUS CONSUMPTION)
3. Some manufacturers deliberately design smartphones to stop working well after two or three years so that customers are forced to buy replacements. (PLANNED OBSOLESCENCE)
4. Schools rarely teach students how to budget, save or understand interest rates before they start earning money. (FINANCIAL LITERACY)
5. Years of relying on credit cards without a repayment plan left the family with debts they could barely manage. (INDEBTEDNESS)
6. Households with a great deal of wealth are often the first to purchase the newest gadgets and luxury cars. (AFFLUENCE)
7. Advertising today constantly promotes the idea that buying more products will make people happier. (CONSUMERIST)
8. A growing number of shoppers are choosing short-term instalment schemes that let them take a product home immediately and pay for it over the following weeks. (BUY-NOW-PAY-LATER)
9. Shoppers tend to judge whether a price is fair based on the very first number they see, even if that number was set arbitrarily by the retailer. (ANCHORING EFFECT)
10. The private tutoring his parents arranged for the entrance exam turned out to be extremely expensive. (COST AN ARM AND A LEG)
11. Many shoppers focus on the pleasure of owning something today and give little thought to how the cost will affect their finances next month. (PRESENT BIAS)
12. Investors frequently hold on to a falling stock for far too long because the pain of accepting the loss feels worse than the pleasure of an equivalent gain would feel. (LOSS AVERSION) ---

Phần A

1. Many young professionals display rampant MATERIALISM, valuing branded possessions far more than experiences or relationships. --- MATERIALISM (noun, uncountable) = chủ nghĩa vật chất; thường đi với "rampant materialism", "rein in materialism"; không dùng dạng số nhiều.

2. Buying an expensive watch just to show colleagues how successful you are is a textbook case of CONSPICUOUS CONSUMPTION. --- CONSPICUOUS CONSUMPTION (noun phrase) = tiêu dùng phô trương; collocation phổ biến: "drive conspicuous consumption", "status-signalling consumption"; không nhầm "conspicuous" (dễ thấy) với "suspicious" (đáng ngờ).

3. Some manufacturers deliberately practise PLANNED OBSOLESCENCE, designing smartphones to stop working well after two or three years so that customers are forced to buy replacements. --- PLANNED OBSOLESCENCE (noun phrase) = lỗi thời có chủ đích; collocation: "a strategy of planned obsolescence", "combat planned obsolescence"; phân biệt với tính từ "obsolete".

4. Schools rarely teach FINANCIAL LITERACY, so students leave without knowing how to budget, save or understand interest rates before they start earning money. --- FINANCIAL LITERACY (noun, uncountable) = hiểu biết tài chính; collocation: "improve/lack of/teach financial literacy"; không đếm được, không có dạng số nhiều.

5. Years of relying on credit cards without a repayment plan left the family grappling with severe INDEBTEDNESS. --- INDEBTEDNESS (noun, uncountable) = tình trạng nợ nần; collocation: "household indebtedness", "mounting indebtedness"; khác "debt" (khoản nợ cụ thể, đếm được).

6. Households of considerable AFFLUENCE are often the first to purchase the newest gadgets and luxury cars. --- AFFLUENCE (noun, uncountable) = sự sung túc, giàu có; collocation: "growing affluence", "a symbol of affluence"; tính từ tương ứng là "affluent", không phải "affluency".

7. Advertising today constantly promotes a CONSUMERIST message, encouraging the idea that buying more products will make people happier. --- CONSUMERIST (adjective) = mang tính chủ nghĩa tiêu dùng; collocation: "a consumerist culture/society/values"; mang sắc thái phê phán, khác "consumer" (danh từ trung tính, người tiêu dùng).

8. A growing number of shoppers are choosing BUY-NOW-PAY-LATER schemes that let them take a product home immediately and pay for it over the following weeks. --- BUY-NOW-PAY-LATER (noun, compound, hyphenated) = mua trước trả sau; luôn viết có gạch nối khi làm danh từ/tính từ ghép ("a buy-now-pay-later scheme"); viết tắt thường gặp: BNPL.

9. Shoppers tend to judge whether a price is fair based on the ANCHORING EFFECT, relying on the very first number they see even if it was set arbitrarily by the retailer. --- ANCHORING EFFECT (noun phrase) = hiệu ứng neo; collocation: "exploit the anchoring effect", "fall prey to anchoring"; luôn đi cùng "effect/bias" khi dùng như thuật ngữ chuyên ngành.

10. The private tutoring his parents arranged for the entrance exam COST AN ARM AND A LEG. --- COST AN ARM AND A LEG (idiom) = đắt cắt cổ; cấu trúc cố định "cost sb an arm and a leg", không thêm số nhiều cho "arm/leg"; phù hợp văn nói hơn văn viết học thuật.

11. Many shoppers exhibit acute PRESENT BIAS, focusing on the pleasure of owning something today and giving little thought to how the cost will affect their finances next month. --- PRESENT BIAS (noun phrase) = thiên kiến hiện tại; collocation: "acute present bias", "exploit present bias"; thuật ngữ behavioural economics, viết liền không gạch nối.

12. Investors frequently hold on to a falling stock for far too long, a textbook symptom of LOSS AVERSION, because the pain of the loss feels worse than the pleasure of an equivalent gain would feel. --- LOSS AVERSION (noun phrase) = tâm lý sợ mất mát; collocation: "exhibit loss aversion", "trigger loss aversion"; khác "risk aversion" (né tránh rủi ro nói chung).
Phần B

1. Band 6: A lot of people spend money on things they don't really need. - Band 7: Many consumers engage in impulse buying, purchasing items they don't genuinely need. - Band 8: Rampant materialism has fostered a culture of conspicuous consumption, in which countless consumers succumb to impulse buying rather than exercising financial restraint.

2. Band 6: It is difficult for poor families to pay for everything they need every month. - Band 7: Many low-income families find it hard to make ends meet on a monthly basis. - Band 8: With disposable income stretched perilously thin, many low-income households are left struggling to make ends meet, let alone build any semblance of a nest egg.

3. Band 6: Some people borrow too much money and then cannot pay it back. - Band 7: Some people take on excessive debt and subsequently struggle to repay it. - Band 8: Mounting household indebtedness can precipitate long-term financial insecurity, particularly among those who live beyond their means without a realistic repayment strategy.

4. Band 6: Shops use clever tricks to make customers buy more than they planned. - Band 7: Retailers exploit psychological tricks, such as the anchoring effect, to encourage customers to spend more than intended. - Band 8: Retailers routinely weaponise cognitive biases, from the anchoring effect to loss aversion, engineering store layouts and pricing with surgical precision to maximise impulse buying.

5. Band 6: Companies make products that break quickly so people have to buy new ones. - Band 7: Companies deliberately manufacture products with a limited lifespan, a strategy known as planned obsolescence, to boost repeat purchases. - Band 8: Many corporations practise planned obsolescence, engineering products to fail shortly after their warranty expires so as to sustain a perpetual cycle of replacement purchases.

6. Band 6: Learning about money at a young age would help people manage their finances better as adults. - Band 7: Improving financial literacy from an early age would help people manage their money more effectively as adults. - Band 8: Embedding financial literacy within the school curriculum from an early age would equip future adults with the conceptual toolkit needed to navigate credit, saving and investment responsibly.

7. Band 6: Digital payment apps make it easy to spend money without noticing how much you have spent. - Band 7: Digital payment apps, including buy-now-pay-later schemes, make it easy for consumers to overspend without realising it. - Band 8: Buy-now-pay-later platforms exploit consumers' present bias, letting the gratification of a purchase arrive instantly while the true cost is conveniently deferred and easily overlooked.

8. Band 6: Rich people sometimes buy expensive things just to show other people how successful they are. - Band 7: Affluent individuals sometimes purchase luxury items purely to display their wealth and status to others. - Band 8: Affluent consumers are increasingly inclined to splurge on conspicuous, status-signalling purchases, a form of materialism that prioritises the perception of success over genuine financial well-being.

passages.text: For most of the second half of the twentieth century, finance textbooks treated the proposition that asset prices fully reflect available information as a foundational result rather than a hypothesis to be defended. A more recent generation of researchers has begun to argue, in the writer's view persuasively, that the efficient-market account survives only in a weaker form than its early advocates assumed, and that behavioural anomalies once dismissed as marginal now sit closer to the heart of how prices actually move. The disagreement matters not only because pensions and retirement savings are at stake, but because the policy institutions that regulate financial markets were calibrated around the stronger reading.

The case for the efficient-market view rests, in the first place, on the difficulty of beating broad indexes after fees. According to Professor Klaus Heller, a financial economist at the University of Frankfurt, longitudinal studies of actively managed funds across roughly forty markets have repeatedly found that the median professional manager underperforms a comparable passive index, particularly once realistic transaction costs are included. Heller's argument is that this finding is harder to reconcile with widespread irrationality than the popular behavioural literature suggests. If prices were systematically mispriced, the case runs, a substantial share of professional investors should be able to identify the mispricings and earn persistent excess returns. The empirical record, on Heller's reading, points in the opposite direction.

The behavioural dimension is no less compelling. A 2023 meta-analysis commissioned by the National Bureau of Economic Research examined four hundred and eleven empirical papers and reported a pattern of well-documented anomalies, including momentum, value premia and the post-earnings-announcement drift, that have survived for several decades after their first identification. The headline finding is widely cited, although Heller cautions that "anomaly" is doing considerable work in the sentence, since some of the patterns shrink once trading costs and survivorship bias are properly modelled. Anomalies that genuinely persist after such adjustments do, however, appear to remain.

The first sustained critique of the strong efficient-market framing has come from Professor Anika Roy, a behavioural finance scholar at Princeton University. Roy has pointed out that aggregate market efficiency, in the technical sense, is consistent with substantial individual irrationality, provided that the irrationalities cancel out across investors. The interesting question, on her account, is whether they cancel out, and her group's analysis of brokerage records from approximately three hundred thousand retail accounts suggests that they do not. Particular biases — including a tendency to sell winners too soon and hold losers too long — appear to operate in the same direction across the majority of accounts she has examined. Roy concedes that this need not produce persistent profit opportunities for sophisticated traders, since arbitrage may close gaps within minutes, but she resists the idea that the behaviour of individual investors is therefore uninteresting.

These two views are not in direct conflict, but they pull research attention in different directions. If the central problem is whether broad markets are roughly efficient at the aggregate level, then the focus belongs on fund performance, fee structures and arbitrage frictions. If, on the other hand, the central problem is how individual investors actually decide, then the focus belongs on biases, framing and the design of choice architecture in retirement accounts and brokerage interfaces. Both interpretations would, in principle, accommodate the same headline figures on index performance, although they disagree on which features of financial behaviour most urgently require attention.

A separate strand of research has focused on the architecture of crises. Researchers in financial history, including Professor Olu Bankole of the African School of Economics in Accra, have argued that the more interesting effect of behavioural pressures may be visible during episodes of stress rather than under ordinary trading conditions. In repeated archival studies of the 2008 banking crisis and the 2020 pandemic-related sell-off, Bankole's group has traced how correlated patterns of selling, driven partly by mechanical risk-control rules and partly by herd behaviour, generated price moves that even sophisticated institutional investors did not predict. The pattern, she argues, is hard to reconcile with the strong efficient-market account, in which such episodes should be self-correcting within days. Whether one labels them anomalies or breakdowns is, she suggests, less interesting than what they reveal about the actual functioning of markets.

As with several other strands of financial research, the most interesting recent work has shifted from the question of which framework is correct to the question of where each framework remains useful. The aggregate efficiency claim works well as a guide to retail investment advice, since the difficulty of beating indexes after fees is genuinely robust. The behavioural account works well as a guide to consumer protection and the design of automatic-enrolment pension schemes, since framing effects on retail accounts are genuinely measurable. Some commentators argue that this division of labour is comfortable enough to settle the dispute. Others, more cautiously, point out that the events of 2008 and 2020 sit uncomfortably with the comfortable division.

A more measured reading sits between the two camps. The aggregate efficiency claim is neither the foundational law it was once taken to be nor a discredited relic. It is a useful approximation under ordinary conditions that becomes misleading under stress, and a research programme taking this dependence seriously is more useful than one defending either side without qualification.

What current research does support is the modest claim that markets aggregate information well enough to make persistent outperformance difficult for most investors, while still leaving room for biases that systematically affect individual decisions and occasionally affect prices on a larger scale. Whether readers find this resolution reassuring or troubling depends on the same question that the original debate raised: how much weight one is willing to place on average behaviour relative to behaviour observed in moments that average least well.

audio_scripts.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is the third in our behavioural-economics research series, and we'll be examining the empirical literature on how households actually allocate discretionary expenditure — and why classical utility models repeatedly fail to predict their behaviour. [pause:5s] The conceptual scaffolding I'll draw on is taken from the work of Professor Hideo Lindqvist — that's L-I-N-D-Q-V-I-S-T; the 'qv' is a Scandinavian cluster pronounced like 'kv'. So Lindqvist. His 2017 monograph reframed household-consumption analysis away from a rational-utility lens into what he calls "mental-account stickiness". [pause:3s] Right. A brief tense-orientation note. Lindqvist's framework USED TO be operationalised through retrospective survey recall only, NOW the field deploys triangulated mixed-methods designs incorporating bank-feed telemetry, supermarket receipt scrapes, and diary-style probes, and from 2027 a multi-country consortium WILL be rolling out continuous biometric-emotion modules. Past, present, future. For today's purposes I'm focusing on the CURRENT methodological state — that is, the bank-feed mixed-methods phase. [pause:3s] The longitudinal cohort I want to reference today was first surveyed in 2019 — sorry, let me correct that, 2018; the published descriptive statistics in 2019 covered baseline data collected in 2018. So whenever I refer to the baseline year for the Adelaide household cohort, please record 2018. [pause:3s] Moving to terminology. The construct Lindqvist foregrounds — the systematic refusal of households to reallocate funds across self-imposed budget envelopes even when reallocation would be objectively optimal — is termed "mental-account stickiness". You'll encounter related labels in the older literature: fungibility friction, ledger inertia, budget compartmentalisation. All of these gesture toward overlapping phenomena, but they are NOT interchangeable with Lindqvist's term. The currently accepted scholarly term is mental-account stickiness — m-e-n-t-a-l hyphen account stickiness. So when the older literature uses fungibility friction or ledger inertia, that's a related but distinct construct. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to discuss is what consumer economists call the "impulse-restraint continuum". When ethnographers describe how households evaluate discretionary purchases under cost-of-living pressure, they sketch a graded continuum running from precommitted denial through deliberative weighing to splurge-cascading. So, you know, you'll see households who pre-set a savings transfer on payday and never touch it — that's precommitted denial. Or households who, kinda, drift into rolling small-ticket splurges through the week — that's splurge-cascading. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical term itself. The umbrella term is the impulse-restraint continuum. [pause:3s] Now, the survey data — and this is where I want you to pay close attention, because the quantifiers cluster densely here. Of the six hundred and forty households we tracked across four Adelaide suburbs last year, MOST exhibited evidence of mental-account stickiness — roughly sixty-eight per cent. Only a few — about twelve per cent — behaved in line with classical fungibility, and some — twenty per cent — produced mixed or context-dependent patterns. So stickiness dominates numerically, but the twelve-per-cent fungibility tail, though small, is theoretically significant. [pause:3s] A second key construct I want to flag is "loss-aversion asymmetry". This refers to the well-documented finding that households weight a one-dollar loss roughly twice as heavily as a one-dollar gain — and this asymmetry intensifies under cost-of-living stress. At the Adelaide site, our analysts documented one hundred and sixty-eight loss-aversion choice episodes across the cohort during one twelve-month tracking window. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that price discounts linearly stimulate consumption is, frankly, not supported. Most of the households in our sample did NOT exhibit the predicted linear uplift in expenditure as discount depth increased. Quite the opposite — many showed a saturation curve, with diminishing response above twenty per cent off. So the older "rational-discount-response" hypothesis, which predicts linear stimulation, is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I made at the start. That CURRENT bank-feed mixed-methods state is what we're, sorta, gonna scrutinise in this afternoon's seminar. I want you to focus on the receipt-scrape protocols specifically, not the biometric-emotion futures or the legacy recall-survey instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: household consumption is best understood through mental-account stickiness, not rational utility; the technical term for the systematic refusal to reallocate across envelopes is mental-account stickiness; stickiness dominates at roughly sixty-eight per cent; and the rational-discount-response hypothesis is not empirically supported in this cohort. Next week we'll examine credit-card revolving behaviour. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

blocks.text: The three pie charts illustrate how an average middle-income family's spending was distributed across six expenditure categories in 1990, 2010 and 2024.

Overall, fixed obligations - namely housing and debt repayment - progressively eclipsed more flexible forms of expenditure, while the proportion set aside as savings contracted sharply. This pattern suggests that the financial latitude of average households was substantially eroded over the three decades.

To begin with, the share devoted to housing and utilities expanded markedly from 24% to 36%, while debt servicing doubled from 9% to 18%, arguably a consequence of pervasive consumer debt and successive rounds of monetary tightening. Conversely, the savings rate plummeted from 16% to a meagre 6%, indicating diminished financial resilience among ordinary families.

Turning to the remaining categories, discretionary spending followed a U-shaped trajectory: it climbed from 14% to 18% by 2010, only to retreat to its original 14% by 2024 amid cost-of-living pressures. Meanwhile, the food and transport shares contracted modestly, from 22% to 14% and from 15% to 12% respectively, likely reflecting efficiency gains rather than any reduction in consumption.
The three pie charts compare the way in which an average middle-income family in a developed economy apportioned its total spending across six categories in 1990, 2010 and 2024.

Overall, what stands out is a steady reallocation from flexible to fixed expenditure: outlays on housing and debt repayment swelled at the expense of savings, which dwindled to a fraction of their former share. The data thus point to a marked erosion of the financial latitude once enjoyed by ordinary households.

The most pronounced movements concern obligatory costs. The housing-and-utilities share climbed inexorably from 24% to 36%, while the proportion absorbed by debt servicing doubled from 9% to 18%, a shift plausibly rooted in mounting consumer debt and successive bouts of monetary tightening. Savings moved in the opposite direction entirely, collapsing from 16% to a slender 6% and leaving families conspicuously exposed to financial shocks.

The discretionary category, by contrast, described a non-monotonic U-curve, advancing from 14% to 18% before subsiding to its original 14% as cost-of-living pressures reasserted themselves. Food and transport, meanwhile, each retreated gently - from 22% to 14% and from 15% to 12% respectively - declines that more likely reflect efficiency gains than genuine belt-tightening on essentials.

blocks.text: As personal debt levels surge across developed economies, the question of who should teach young people about money has climbed the policy agenda. While many parents believe that money management is a household matter, a growing chorus argues that financial literacy belongs in the formal curriculum. On balance, I side with the latter view, although the home certainly retains an important supporting role.

Advocates of the home-based approach reason that money habits are typically caught rather than taught. Children observe their parents budgeting, saving and resisting impulse buying long before they encounter a textbook. Moreover, family values around debt, generosity and conspicuous consumption vary widely, which arguably makes one-size-fits-all classroom teaching ineffective. From this perspective, schools risk replacing rich, contextual learning with bland, generic content.

Nevertheless, leaving the matter entirely to households tends to entrench existing inequalities. It is precisely the children of low-income families, whose parents may themselves struggle to make ends meet, who most need structured instruction on interest rates, taxes and credit. Schools can also counter the relentless behavioural nudges that modern advertising deploys; without formal training, students often fall prey to predatory 'Buy Now, Pay Later' schemes that exploit cognitive biases. A compulsory subject would further ensure that essentials such as compound interest and inflation are not left to chance.

In conclusion, although parental modelling clearly matters, schools are better positioned to deliver consistent, evidence-based financial education. What policymakers should do is integrate practical modules on budgeting and debt into secondary curricula while encouraging parents to reinforce these lessons at home. Treating financial literacy as a partnership, rather than an either-or choice, would produce the most resilient young consumers.

How effectively young adults manage credit, savings and consumption now ranks among the strongest predictors of lifelong well-being. Whether such competence should be cultivated through formal schooling or left to the household is therefore a question of genuine consequence. Having weighed both arguments, I lean firmly towards making financial literacy a compulsory school subject, while acknowledging that parental modelling remains indispensable.

Those who favour the domestic route reason that monetary habits are deeply tacit, absorbed by daily observation rather than transmitted in a forty-five-minute lesson. There is much to this. Cultural and religious attitudes towards debt vary so widely that a uniform syllabus risks flattening valuable diversity. Moreover, what households teach by example - delayed gratification, prudent budgeting, resistance to status consumption - tends to outweigh any textbook intervention in shaping enduring behaviour.

However, relying exclusively on the home effectively outsources a public-policy problem to the very families least equipped to solve it. Households grappling with stagnant wages and rising precarity are unlikely to model sound finance; nor can they realistically counter the dark patterns embedded in fintech apps and 'Buy Now, Pay Later' platforms. What contemporary behavioural economics demonstrates is that present-bias and loss aversion systematically distort everyday choices, often nudging consumers towards overspending. Only a structured curriculum, ideally integrated with mathematics and citizenship, appears capable of equipping students to recognise and resist these manipulations.

Nor is the case purely defensive: financial literacy correlates strongly with retirement readiness, entrepreneurial activity and democratic participation. In conclusion, although the home will always be the first classroom of money, it cannot, on its own, neutralise systemic commercial pressures. What modern economies require is a deliberate, compulsory pedagogical foundation, complemented - not replaced - by parental example. Anything less effectively concedes the field to predatory finance.

solutions.text: PHẦN A — Viết lại câu (12 items)
Viết lại mỗi câu dưới đây dùng TỪ GỢI Ý (in hoa), giữ nguyên nghĩa và đúng dạng/collocation.
1. Many young professionals value owning branded possessions far more than they value experiences or relationships. (MATERIALISM)
2. Buying an expensive watch just to show colleagues how successful you are is a very obvious example of this kind of spending. (CONSPICUOUS CONSUMPTION)
3. Some manufacturers deliberately design smartphones to stop working well after two or three years so that customers are forced to buy replacements. (PLANNED OBSOLESCENCE)
4. Schools rarely teach students how to budget, save or understand interest rates before they start earning money. (FINANCIAL LITERACY)
5. Years of relying on credit cards without a repayment plan left the family with debts they could barely manage. (INDEBTEDNESS)
6. Households with a great deal of wealth are often the first to purchase the newest gadgets and luxury cars. (AFFLUENCE)
7. Advertising today constantly promotes the idea that buying more products will make people happier. (CONSUMERIST)
8. A growing number of shoppers are choosing short-term instalment schemes that let them take a product home immediately and pay for it over the following weeks. (BUY-NOW-PAY-LATER)
9. Shoppers tend to judge whether a price is fair based on the very first number they see, even if that number was set arbitrarily by the retailer. (ANCHORING EFFECT)
10. The private tutoring his parents arranged for the entrance exam turned out to be extremely expensive. (COST AN ARM AND A LEG)
11. Many shoppers focus on the pleasure of owning something today and give little thought to how the cost will affect their finances next month. (PRESENT BIAS)
12. Investors frequently hold on to a falling stock for far too long because the pain of accepting the loss feels worse than the pleasure of an equivalent gain would feel. (LOSS AVERSION) ---

1. Many young professionals display rampant MATERIALISM, valuing branded possessions far more than experiences or relationships. --- MATERIALISM (noun, uncountable) = chủ nghĩa vật chất; thường đi với "rampant materialism", "rein in materialism"; không dùng dạng số nhiều.

2. Buying an expensive watch just to show colleagues how successful you are is a textbook case of CONSPICUOUS CONSUMPTION. --- CONSPICUOUS CONSUMPTION (noun phrase) = tiêu dùng phô trương; collocation phổ biến: "drive conspicuous consumption", "status-signalling consumption"; không nhầm "conspicuous" (dễ thấy) với "suspicious" (đáng ngờ).

3. Some manufacturers deliberately practise PLANNED OBSOLESCENCE, designing smartphones to stop working well after two or three years so that customers are forced to buy replacements. --- PLANNED OBSOLESCENCE (noun phrase) = lỗi thời có chủ đích; collocation: "a strategy of planned obsolescence", "combat planned obsolescence"; phân biệt với tính từ "obsolete".

4. Schools rarely teach FINANCIAL LITERACY, so students leave without knowing how to budget, save or understand interest rates before they start earning money. --- FINANCIAL LITERACY (noun, uncountable) = hiểu biết tài chính; collocation: "improve/lack of/teach financial literacy"; không đếm được, không có dạng số nhiều.

5. Years of relying on credit cards without a repayment plan left the family grappling with severe INDEBTEDNESS. --- INDEBTEDNESS (noun, uncountable) = tình trạng nợ nần; collocation: "household indebtedness", "mounting indebtedness"; khác "debt" (khoản nợ cụ thể, đếm được).

6. Households of considerable AFFLUENCE are often the first to purchase the newest gadgets and luxury cars. --- AFFLUENCE (noun, uncountable) = sự sung túc, giàu có; collocation: "growing affluence", "a symbol of affluence"; tính từ tương ứng là "affluent", không phải "affluency".

7. The Credit Card Debt Crisis: In many developed nations, consumer debt has reached record highs due to the normalisation of "Buy Now, Pay Later" schemes, trapping young adults in endless cycles of debt.
The Minimalist Movement: A growing counter-culture trend rejecting materialism; it advocates for owning fewer possessions to focus on experiences, mental well-being, and environmental sustainability.

Targeted Advertising (Algorithms): Social media platforms use highly sophisticated algorithms to track user behaviour, presenting hyper-targeted ads that drastically increase the likelihood of impulse buying.
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Does Money Buy Happiness?

Arguments FOR (Up to a point): Money eliminates financial stress (worrying about making ends meet); it provides access to premium healthcare, nutritious food, and quality education; it buys "time" and freedom.

Arguments AGAINST: Beyond a certain threshold (covering basic needs), acquiring more wealth yields diminishing returns in happiness (the Hedonic Treadmill); rampant materialism often leads to social alienation and superficial relationships.
Topic: Youth Debt & Financial Literacy

Causes of Youth Debt: Schools entirely neglect teaching practical financial literacy (budgeting, taxes, interest rates); relentless peer pressure to acquire the latest status symbols (smartphones, designer clothes).

Solutions: Governments must integrate mandatory personal finance courses into the high school curriculum; stricter regulations should be imposed on predatory lending companies targeting vulnerable students.
Topic: The Impact of Consumerism on Society and Environment
Negative Effects on Individuals: Encourages a culture of greed and perpetual dissatisfaction; people work excessively long hours just to fund conspicuous consumption, leading to severe burnout.

Negative Effects on Environment: Mass production and planned obsolescence generate mountains of non-biodegradable waste; the extraction of raw materials to fuel consumer demands causes catastrophic deforestation and pollution.

Model Answer (Band 7.5-8.0, ~270 words)

The financial habit I'd like to discuss is what behavioural economists call "paying yourself first" — automatically transferring a fixed percentage of every paycheque into a separate investment account before any discretionary spending occurs. I've been practising it consistently since roughly 2019, and it has, without exaggeration, transformed my relationship with money.

The origins of the habit trace back to reading Morgan Housel's "The Psychology of Money" during the pandemic lull. What struck me was his observation that wealth-building is far less about income and far more about the gap between earnings and ego-driven consumption. Inspired by this, I set up an automated standing order channelling 25% of my monthly salary into an index fund tracking the VN30, with a smaller tranche allocated to a US ETF for geographic diversification.

The mechanism itself is deceptively simple, but its psychological elegance lies in removing willpower from the equation. Rarely do I see the money in my main account, so the temptation toward impulse buying — the cognitive trap that retail therapy exploits — is neutralised at the source. What this circumvents is precisely the kind of "dark patterns" that modern fintech apps deploy to keep users perpetually spending.

The benefits have been threefold. Firstly, in five years I've accumulated a nest egg sufficient to cover roughly fourteen months of expenses, which materially insulates me from precarity. Secondly, the habit forced me to live well within my means, dispelling the illusion that lifestyle inflation was inevitable. Thirdly, and perhaps most importantly, it instilled a long-term mindset that has bled into other domains — career planning, health, relationships.
In retrospect, automating that single decision was probably the most consequential financial choice I've ever made.

blocks.text: Q1: Is a cashless society better?

Point: While the convenience of cashless payment is undeniable, I'd argue that a fully cashless society carries genuine downsides that policymakers tend to underplay — so a hybrid model remains preferable for the foreseeable future.

Explain: What cashlessness fundamentally does is concentrate transactional power in the hands of a few payment intermediaries and central banks, which raises significant concerns around financial surveillance, exclusion of unbanked populations, and systemic fragility during outages. Cash, for all its inefficiencies, offers anonymity and resilience.

Example: Sweden, the poster child of cashless adoption, has seen its Riksbank quietly walk back its earlier enthusiasm, citing concerns about elderly citizens being excluded and the vulnerability of digital infrastructure — a recent parliamentary report explicitly recommended preserving cash access. Conversely, Vietnam's QR-code revolution, with VietQR processing over 1.7 billion transactions in 2023, has democratised payments without eliminating physical currency, which seems a sensible middle path.
Link: So rather than racing to abolish cash entirely, governments would be wiser to preserve optionality, ensuring digital inclusion doesn't translate into digital coercion.
Q2: Should financial education be earlier?
Point: Absolutely — and I'd argue that the persistent failure to integrate financial literacy into primary and secondary curricula is one of the more glaring omissions of modern education systems.

Explain: The core issue is that financial decisions — managing credit, understanding compound interest, evaluating insurance — have become exponentially more complex, yet most teenagers graduate without the conceptual toolkit to navigate them. This vacuum is precisely what predatory lenders and "Buy Now, Pay Later" schemes exploit.

Example: A 2022 OECD study found that financial literacy among adults averaged just 60% across member states, with younger demographics scoring particularly poorly on questions involving risk and diversification. By contrast, the UK's introduction of mandatory financial education in 2014, while imperfect in execution, has been associated with measurably better budgeting behaviours among young adults. Singapore's MoneySense programme starts as early as primary school and is widely regarded as best-in-class.
Link: So integrating financial literacy from age ten onwards isn't a luxury but a basic civic competence — and its absence costs societies dearly in household debt and bankruptcy.
Q3: Are cryptocurrencies a good investment?

Point: Cryptocurrencies, in my honest view, occupy a genuinely speculative niche rather than a credible long-term investment for the average household — though I wouldn't go so far as to dismiss the underlying technology.

Explain: The fundamental problem is volatility: assets like Bitcoin routinely swing 20-30% within weeks, which is incompatible with most retail investors' risk tolerance. Worse, the sector remains plagued by fraud, regulatory ambiguity, and an opaque architecture that retail buyers rarely understand.

Example: The 2022 collapse of FTX, which evaporated $8 billion of customer funds, exemplifies the precarity baked into the ecosystem — and the subsequent contagion wiped roughly $2 trillion from global crypto market capitalisation. Even Bitcoin, the most established asset, fell from $69,000 to below $16,000 within twelve months. By contrast, a diversified equity index fund returned roughly 10% annually over the past decade, with a fraction of the volatility.
Link: So while a tiny speculative allocation might be defensible for those who genuinely understand the risks, treating crypto as a retirement strategy is, to put it bluntly, financial recklessness.

4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Good afternoon. Today I want to thread together three strands that household-finance debates routinely treat in isolation: behavioural economics, consumer debt and monetary policy. Properly understood, they are deeply interlocking mechanisms.

> Let us begin with behavioural economics, brought to prominence by the Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman and his collaborator Amos Tversky. Their work overturned the homo economicus model — the fiction of the calmly rational consumer. We are, in fact, governed by present bias, anchoring effects, loss aversion and the endowment effect. Retailers and lenders have weaponised these heuristics with surgical precision, from the placement of confectionery at checkout aisles to the framing of "minimum monthly payment" on credit-card statements.

> Now, consumer debt. In the United States, household debt breached seventeen trillion dollars in 2023, with credit-card balances alone exceeding one trillion. The most aggressive growth, however, is in buy-now-pay-later schemes — services such as Klarna and Afterpay — which sidestep traditional credit checks and exploit younger consumers' acute present bias. The Bank of England has warned of an emergent shadow consumer-credit ecosystem invisible to conventional risk modelling.

> Finally, monetary policy. When central banks raise the base rate, they aim to cool demand and tame inflation. But the transmission mechanism is uneven: mortgage holders feel the pinch immediately, while affluent savers benefit, and the truly debt-saturated household cannot easily refinance at all. The Australian Reserve Bank economist Philip Lowe conceded in 2023 that monetary policy is "a blunt instrument with distributional consequences".

Now, before we plot those debt-to-income ratios, I want to dwell on a mechanism that ties my three strands together even more tightly than I first let on — and that is the architecture of money itself, or rather, the disappearance of money's friction. Think about what cash used to do. Handing over physical notes registers, psychologically, as a loss; you feel the wallet thin. The behavioural literature calls this the "pain of paying", and Drazen Prelec's neuroimaging work at MIT actually located it — spending activates regions associated with physical discomfort. [pause] Now, every innovation in payments since has been, whether intended or not, an exercise in anaesthetising that pain.

Contactless cards removed the act of counting. One-click checkout removed the act of deciding. And buy-now-pay-later, well, it does something more insidious still: it severs the purchase from the payment entirely in time, so the dopamine of acquisition arrives today while the cost is exiled to a future self the present self barely cares about. That is present bias, industrialised. The frictionlessness is not a convenience side-effect; it is, increasingly, the product.

Here is a finding that ought to unsettle us. Studies of mobile-payment adoption suggest consumers systematically underestimate their cumulative spending when transactions are digital and disaggregated into small, frequent taps. The mental accounting fragments; no single tap feels consequential, yet the aggregate balloons. [pause] Um, and the younger the cohort, the more pronounced the effect, precisely the demographic that BNPL targets.

So when the central bank raises rates to cool an overheated economy, it is pulling a lever calibrated for a world of deliberate, friction-laden borrowing — while the actual borrowing happens in a frictionless interface engineered to bypass deliberation altogether. The macroeconomic instrument and the microeconomic reality are, quite simply, out of phase. That mismatch is exactly what the regulatory discussion after this must grapple with, because the question becomes whether…

> The take-home is uncomfortable: macroeconomic levers cannot offset microeconomic manipulation. We need behavioural regulation alongside interest-rate orthodoxy. Now, turning to figure two, which plots household debt-to-income ratios…

blocks.text: (e) Bài mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~179 từ)
The three pie charts illustrate how an average middle-income family's spending was distributed across six expenditure categories in 1990, 2010 and 2024.

Overall, fixed obligations - namely housing and debt repayment - progressively eclipsed more flexible forms of expenditure, while the proportion set aside as savings contracted sharply. This pattern suggests that the financial latitude of average households was substantially eroded over the three decades.

To begin with, the share devoted to housing and utilities expanded markedly from 24% to 36%, while debt servicing doubled from 9% to 18%, arguably a consequence of pervasive consumer debt and successive rounds of monetary tightening. Conversely, the savings rate plummeted from 16% to a meagre 6%, indicating diminished financial resilience among ordinary families.

Turning to the remaining categories, discretionary spending followed a U-shaped trajectory: it climbed from 14% to 18% by 2010, only to retreat to its original 14% by 2024 amid cost-of-living pressures. Meanwhile, the food and transport shares contracted modestly, from 22% to 14% and from 15% to 12% respectively, likely reflecting efficiency gains rather than any reduction in consumption.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~200 từ)
The three pie charts compare the way in which an average middle-income family in a developed economy apportioned its total spending across six categories in 1990, 2010 and 2024.

Overall, what stands out is a steady reallocation from flexible to fixed expenditure: outlays on housing and debt repayment swelled at the expense of savings, which dwindled to a fraction of their former share. The data thus point to a marked erosion of the financial latitude once enjoyed by ordinary households.

The most pronounced movements concern obligatory costs. The housing-and-utilities share climbed inexorably from 24% to 36%, while the proportion absorbed by debt servicing doubled from 9% to 18%, a shift plausibly rooted in mounting consumer debt and successive bouts of monetary tightening. Savings moved in the opposite direction entirely, collapsing from 16% to a slender 6% and leaving families conspicuously exposed to financial shocks.

The discretionary category, by contrast, described a non-monotonic U-curve, advancing from 14% to 18% before subsiding to its original 14% as cost-of-living pressures reasserted themselves. Food and transport, meanwhile, each retreated gently - from 22% to 14% and from 15% to 12% respectively - declines that more likely reflect efficiency gains than genuine belt-tightening on essentials.
(g) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8
•  Band 8 mở overview bằng cấu trúc nhấn mạnh ('what stands out is a steady reallocation...') và khái quát xu hướng cốt lõi (flexible -> fixed), thay vì liệt kê rời rạc như Band 7.
•  Band 8 dùng động từ và lexis sống động, chính xác hơn ('swelled', 'dwindled', 'climbed inexorably', 'collapsing to a slender 6%', 'non-monotonic U-curve') nâng Lexical Resource một bậc.
•  Band 8 kiểm soát mọi số liệu khớp dữ liệu (24->36, 9->18, 16->6, 14->18->14, 22->14, 15->12) trong câu phức nhiều mệnh đề, thể hiện Grammatical Range và độ chính xác vượt Band 7.
(h) Chiến lược làm bài (5 bước)

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~273 words)

As personal debt levels surge across developed economies, the question of who should teach young people about money has climbed the policy agenda. While many parents believe that money management is a household matter, a growing chorus argues that financial literacy belongs in the formal curriculum. On balance, I side with the latter view, although the home certainly retains an important supporting role.

Advocates of the home-based approach reason that money habits are typically caught rather than taught. Children observe their parents budgeting, saving and resisting impulse buying long before they encounter a textbook. Moreover, family values around debt, generosity and conspicuous consumption vary widely, which arguably makes one-size-fits-all classroom teaching ineffective. From this perspective, schools risk replacing rich, contextual learning with bland, generic content.

Nevertheless, leaving the matter entirely to households tends to entrench existing inequalities. It is precisely the children of low-income families, whose parents may themselves struggle to make ends meet, who most need structured instruction on interest rates, taxes and credit. Schools can also counter the relentless behavioural nudges that modern advertising deploys; without formal training, students often fall prey to predatory 'Buy Now, Pay Later' schemes that exploit cognitive biases. A compulsory subject would further ensure that essentials such as compound interest and inflation are not left to chance.

In conclusion, although parental modelling clearly matters, schools are better positioned to deliver consistent, evidence-based financial education. What policymakers should do is integrate practical modules on budgeting and debt into secondary curricula while encouraging parents to reinforce these lessons at home. Treating financial literacy as a partnership, rather than an either-or choice, would produce the most resilient young consumers.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~293 words)

How effectively young adults manage credit, savings and consumption now ranks among the strongest predictors of lifelong well-being. Whether such competence should be cultivated through formal schooling or left to the household is therefore a question of genuine consequence. Having weighed both arguments, I lean firmly towards making financial literacy a compulsory school subject, while acknowledging that parental modelling remains indispensable.

Those who favour the domestic route reason that monetary habits are deeply tacit, absorbed by daily observation rather than transmitted in a forty-five-minute lesson. There is much to this. Cultural and religious attitudes towards debt vary so widely that a uniform syllabus risks flattening valuable diversity. Moreover, what households teach by example - delayed gratification, prudent budgeting, resistance to status consumption - tends to outweigh any textbook intervention in shaping enduring behaviour.

However, relying exclusively on the home effectively outsources a public-policy problem to the very families least equipped to solve it. Households grappling with stagnant wages and rising precarity are unlikely to model sound finance; nor can they realistically counter the dark patterns embedded in fintech apps and 'Buy Now, Pay Later' platforms. What contemporary behavioural economics demonstrates is that present-bias and loss aversion systematically distort everyday choices, often nudging consumers towards overspending. Only a structured curriculum, ideally integrated with mathematics and citizenship, appears capable of equipping students to recognise and resist these manipulations.

Nor is the case purely defensive: financial literacy correlates strongly with retirement readiness, entrepreneurial activity and democratic participation. In conclusion, although the home will always be the first classroom of money, it cannot, on its own, neutralise systemic commercial pressures. What modern economies require is a deliberate, compulsory pedagogical foundation, complemented - not replaced - by parental example. Anything less effectively concedes the field to predatory finance.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dùng cấu trúc phức cao cấp xuyên suốt (inversion 'Nor is the case purely defensive', cleft 'What contemporary behavioural economics demonstrates is...', 'What modern economies require is...') trong khi Band 7 chỉ dùng một vài lần.
•  Band 8 dẫn khái niệm chuyên sâu hơn ('present-bias', 'loss aversion', 'dark patterns', 'retirement readiness') và nominalisation dày đặc, nâng Lexical Resource và chiều sâu Task Response.

•  Band 8 có cohesion tinh tế và register học thuật nhất quán ('There is much to this', 'nor can they realistically...'), loại bỏ cụm hơi đời thường như 'bland, generic content' và 'caught rather than taught' của bản 7.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tằn tiện, cẩn trọng với tiền bạc, tránh chi tiêu không cần thiết.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Adopting a more **frugal** lifestyle can provide a valuable buffer against economic shocks.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'frugal' nghe gần 'thrifty' → người tằn tiện luôn cân nhắc từng đồng.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Frugal' mang sắc thái tích cực (khôn ngoan, tiết kiệm hợp lý), khác với 'stingy/miserly' (keo kiệt, mang nghĩa tiêu cực) — đừng dùng thay thế cho nhau.
vocabulary.definition_en: careful and sparing with money; avoiding unnecessary spending
vocabulary.definition_vi: tằn tiện, tiết kiệm
vocabulary.example: Adopting a more frugal lifestyle can provide a valuable buffer against economic shocks.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'frugal' nghe gần 'thrifty' → người tằn tiện luôn cân nhắc từng đồng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tình trạng nợ nần, mắc nợ tài chính ở mức đáng lo ngại.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Mounting household **indebtedness** can precipitate long-term financial insecurity.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
in- (ở trong) + debt (nợ) + -edness → trạng thái chìm trong nợ.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Indebtedness' là danh từ trừu tượng chỉ tình trạng chung, khác với 'debt' (khoản nợ cụ thể, có thể đếm được) — 'indebtedness' hầu như luôn không đếm được.
vocabulary.definition_en: the state of owing money to someone or having significant financial debt
vocabulary.definition_vi: tình trạng nợ nần
vocabulary.example: Mounting household indebtedness can precipitate long-term financial insecurity.
vocabulary.memory_hook: in- (ở trong) + debt (nợ) + -edness → trạng thái chìm trong nợ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự sung túc, giàu có về tiền bạc và tiện nghi vật chất.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Affluent** consumers are increasingly inclined to splurge on conspicuous, status-signalling purchases.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
af- + fluere (gốc Latin "chảy vào") → tiền của chảy vào đầy ắp → sung túc.
vocabulary.common_error: Danh từ là 'affluence', tính từ là 'affluent' — học viên hay viết nhầm 'affluency'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the state of having a great deal of money, wealth or material comfort
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự sung túc, giàu có
vocabulary.example: Affluent consumers are increasingly inclined to splurge on conspicuous, status-signalling purchases.
vocabulary.memory_hook: af- + fluere (gốc Latin 'chảy vào') → tiền của chảy vào đầy ắp → sung túc.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hoang phí, chi tiêu vượt quá mức cần thiết hoặc khả năng chi trả.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> That authentic designer handbag was an **extravagant** purchase, costing an arm and a leg.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
extra- (vượt quá) + vagant (đi lang thang) → chi tiêu "đi lạc" vượt quá mức cần thiết.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Extravagant' chỉ hành vi chi tiêu (người/lối sống), tránh nhầm với 'extraordinary' (phi thường) dù hai từ có phần đầu gần giống.
vocabulary.definition_en: spending much more money than is necessary or than one can afford
vocabulary.definition_vi: hoang phí, xa hoa quá mức
vocabulary.example: That authentic designer handbag was an extravagant purchase, costing an arm and a leg.
vocabulary.memory_hook: extra- (vượt quá) + vagant (đi lang thang) → chi tiêu 'đi lạc' vượt quá mức cần thiết.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Mang tính chủ nghĩa tiêu dùng, thúc đẩy việc mua sắm và tiêu thụ liên tục.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Pervasive advertising relentlessly stokes consumer desire, fuelling a **consumerist**, throwaway culture.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
consumer (người tiêu dùng) + -ist → mang tư tưởng đề cao tiêu dùng.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Consumerist' (tính từ, mang tính phê phán về văn hóa tiêu dùng) khác với 'consumer' (danh từ chỉ người tiêu dùng, trung tính) — không thay thế cho nhau.
vocabulary.definition_en: relating to or promoting the constant buying and consuming of goods
vocabulary.definition_vi: thuộc về/mang tính chủ nghĩa tiêu dùng
vocabulary.example: Pervasive advertising relentlessly stokes consumer desire, fuelling a consumerist, throwaway culture.
vocabulary.memory_hook: consumer (người tiêu dùng) + -ist → mang tư tưởng đề cao tiêu dùng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hình thức mua trước trả sau, một dạng tín dụng ngắn hạn cho phép trả góp mà thường không tính lãi.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The most aggressive growth in household debt is in **buy-now-pay-later** schemes, which sidestep traditional credit checks and exploit younger consumers' acute present bias.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
buy now (mua ngay) + pay later (trả sau) → mua trước, trả góp sau, thường không lãi suất.
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm này luôn viết có gạch nối khi làm danh từ/tính từ ghép ('a buy-now-pay-later scheme'); thường viết tắt là 'BNPL' trong văn phong báo chí tài chính.
vocabulary.definition_en: a short-term credit scheme that lets consumers pay for a purchase in instalments, typically without upfront interest
vocabulary.definition_vi: hình thức 'mua trước trả sau' (trả góp ngắn hạn, thường không tính lãi)
vocabulary.example: The most aggressive growth in household debt is in buy-now-pay-later schemes, which sidestep traditional credit checks and exploit younger consumers' acute present bias.
vocabulary.memory_hook: buy now (mua ngay) + pay later (trả sau) → mua trước, trả góp sau, thường không lãi suất.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vật lộn, cố gắng xử lý một vấn đề hay thách thức khó khăn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Experts **grapple with** the challenge of regulating predatory fintech apps, often at the expense of vulnerable consumers.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'grapple' nghe như 'grip' + 'struggle' → nắm chặt vật lộn với vấn đề khó.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn đi với giới từ 'with': 'grapple with sth', không phải 'grapple sth' hay 'grapple on sth'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to try hard to deal with or understand a difficult problem or issue
vocabulary.definition_vi: vật lộn/đương đầu với (một vấn đề khó khăn)
vocabulary.example: Experts grapple with the challenge of regulating predatory fintech apps, often at the expense of vulnerable consumers.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'grapple' nghe như 'grip' + 'struggle' → nắm chặt vật lộn với vấn đề khó.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hiệu ứng neo, thiên kiến nhận thức khi con người dựa quá nhiều vào thông tin đầu tiên nhận được lúc ra quyết định.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> We are, in fact, governed by present bias, **anchoring effects**, loss aversion and the endowment effect, which retailers have weaponised with surgical precision.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
anchor (mỏ neo) → thông tin đầu tiên như một "cái neo" giữ chặt phán đoán của ta lại, khó điều chỉnh.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Anchoring' trong kinh tế học hành vi là danh động từ chỉ thiên kiến nhận thức, khác nghĩa đen 'neo tàu'; luôn đi với 'effect/bias' khi làm thuật ngữ chuyên ngành.
vocabulary.definition_en: a cognitive bias in which people rely too heavily on the first piece of information offered when making decisions
vocabulary.definition_vi: hiệu ứng neo (thiên kiến dựa quá nhiều vào thông tin đầu tiên khi ra quyết định)
vocabulary.example: We are, in fact, governed by present bias, anchoring effects, loss aversion and the endowment effect, which retailers have weaponised with surgical precision.
vocabulary.memory_hook: anchor (mỏ neo) → thông tin đầu tiên như một 'cái neo' giữ chặt phán đoán của ta lại, khó điều chỉnh.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Xoay xở đủ sống, kiếm đủ tiền để trang trải các nhu cầu cơ bản.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> With the rising cost of living, many low-income families are struggling to **make ends meet**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
hình dung thu nhập và chi tiêu là hai đầu dây (ends) phải chạm được vào nhau (meet) mới đủ sống.
collocations: find it hard to make ends meet
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm này luôn ở dạng 'make ends meet' (không chia số ít 'end'); dùng với 'struggle to' hoặc 'find it hard to' phía trước.
vocabulary.definition_en: to have just enough money to pay for the things one needs
vocabulary.definition_vi: xoay xở đủ sống, kiếm đủ tiền trang trải
vocabulary.example: With the rising cost of living, many low-income families are struggling to make ends meet.
vocabulary.memory_hook: hình dung thu nhập và chi tiêu là hai đầu dây (ends) phải chạm được vào nhau (meet) mới đủ sống.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sống vượt quá khả năng chi trả, tiêu tiền nhiều hơn số tiền kiếm được.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> He spends much more money than he actually earns, effectively **living beyond his means**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'means' = khả năng tài chính → sống "vượt" (beyond) khả năng đó → tiêu quá mức kiếm được.
collocations: the dangers of living beyond one's means
vocabulary.common_error: 'Means' trong cụm này luôn ở số nhiều và mang nghĩa 'khả năng tài chính', khác với nghĩa 'phương tiện' thông thường của từ 'means'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to spend more money than one earns or can afford
vocabulary.definition_vi: sống vượt quá khả năng chi trả (chi tiêu nhiều hơn thu nhập)
vocabulary.example: He spends much more money than he actually earns, effectively living beyond his means.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'means' = khả năng tài chính → sống 'vượt' (beyond) khả năng đó → tiêu quá mức kiếm được.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đắt cắt cổ, cực kỳ đắt đỏ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> That luxury watch **cost an arm and a leg**, yet he bought it without a second thought.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
tưởng tượng phải trả giá bằng cả một cánh tay và một cái chân → cái giá quá đắt.
collocations: cost sb an arm and a leg
pay an arm and a leg for sth
vocabulary.common_error: Đây là idiom, không được thêm mạo từ hay số nhiều cho 'arm'/'leg' (không nói 'an arm and legs'); phù hợp văn nói/Speaking hơn Writing học thuật.
vocabulary.definition_en: to be extremely expensive
vocabulary.definition_vi: đắt cắt cổ, đắt kinh khủng
vocabulary.example: That luxury watch cost an arm and a leg, yet he bought it without a second thought.
vocabulary.headword: Cost an arm and a leg
vocabulary.memory_hook: tưởng tượng phải trả giá bằng cả một cánh tay và một cái chân → cái giá quá đắt.
vocabulary.syllables: cost an ARM and a LEG

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Khoản tiền tích lũy dự phòng, thường để dành cho hưu trí hoặc lúc khẩn cấp.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Over the years, they have built up a substantial **nest egg** for their comfortable retirement.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'nest egg' vốn là quả trứng để lại trong ổ để dụ gà đẻ tiếp → tiền để dành "nuôi lớn" cho tương lai.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Nest egg' luôn dùng như danh từ chỉ khoản tiết kiệm cụ thể, đi cùng động từ 'build up/accumulate', không dùng với 'save a nest egg'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a sum of money saved for the future, especially for retirement or emergencies
vocabulary.definition_vi: khoản tiền tích lũy dự phòng (tiết kiệm cho tương lai)
vocabulary.example: Over the years, they have built up a substantial nest egg for their comfortable retirement.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'nest egg' vốn là quả trứng để lại trong ổ để dụ gà đẻ tiếp → tiền để dành 'nuôi lớn' cho tương lai.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sinh ra đã ngậm thìa vàng, tức được sinh ra trong một gia đình giàu có, hưởng đặc quyền từ nhỏ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> He doesn't understand the struggles of poverty because he was **born with a silver spoon in his mouth**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
trẻ nhà giàu xưa được cho ngậm thìa bạc lúc mới sinh, khác trẻ nhà nghèo dùng thìa gỗ → biểu tượng của sự giàu có bẩm sinh.
collocations: born with a silver spoon in one's mouth
vocabulary.common_error: Idiom cố định, không đổi 'silver' thành từ khác; thường dùng ở thì quá khứ bị động 'was/were born with...'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to be born into a wealthy family and enjoy privilege from birth
vocabulary.definition_vi: sinh ra đã ngậm thìa vàng (sinh ra trong gia đình giàu có)
vocabulary.example: He doesn't understand the struggles of poverty because he was born with a silver spoon in his mouth.
vocabulary.headword: Born with a silver spoon in one's mouth
vocabulary.memory_hook: trẻ nhà giàu xưa được cho ngậm thìa bạc lúc mới sinh, khác trẻ nhà nghèo dùng thìa gỗ → biểu tượng của sự giàu có bẩm sinh.
vocabulary.pronunciation: /bɔːn wɪð ə ˈsɪl.vər spuːn ɪn wʌnz maʊθ/

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chịu trách nhiệm thanh toán một khoản chi phí, thường là hậu quả do người khác gây ra.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> When the government makes economic mistakes, it is usually the taxpayers who have to **foot the bill**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'foot' cũng có nghĩa cổ là "cộng tổng số tiền ở cuối hóa đơn" → foot the bill = đứng ra trả hóa đơn đó.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Foot' ở đây là động từ (trả tiền), không phải danh từ 'bàn chân' — học viên hay hiểu nhầm nghĩa đen.
vocabulary.definition_en: to pay for something, especially an expense caused by someone else
vocabulary.definition_vi: chịu trách nhiệm thanh toán, trả hóa đơn (thường do lỗi của người khác)
vocabulary.example: When the government makes economic mistakes, it is usually the taxpayers who have to foot the bill.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'foot' cũng có nghĩa cổ là 'cộng tổng số tiền ở cuối hóa đơn' → foot the bill = đứng ra trả hóa đơn đó.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thiên kiến hiện tại, xu hướng ưu tiên phần thưởng trước mắt hơn lợi ích trong tương lai.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Buy-now-pay-later schemes exploit younger consumers' acute **present bias**, letting the dopamine of acquisition arrive today while the cost is exiled to the future.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
present (hiện tại) + bias (thiên lệch) → não bộ "thiên vị" cho cái lợi ngay bây giờ.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Present bias' là thuật ngữ chuyên ngành behavioural economics, luôn viết liền không gạch nối; đừng nhầm với nghĩa thông thường của 'present' (quà tặng).
vocabulary.definition_en: a systematic tendency to overweight immediate rewards over future ones when making decisions
vocabulary.definition_vi: thiên kiến hiện tại (xu hướng ưu tiên lợi ích trước mắt hơn lợi ích tương lai)
vocabulary.example: Buy-now-pay-later schemes exploit younger consumers' acute present bias, letting the dopamine of acquisition arrive today while the cost is exiled to the future.
vocabulary.memory_hook: present (hiện tại) + bias (thiên lệch) → não bộ 'thiên vị' cho cái lợi ngay bây giờ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tâm lý sợ mất mát, khi cảm giác mất mát tác động mạnh hơn nhiều so với cảm giác đạt được tương đương.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> What contemporary behavioural economics demonstrates is that **loss aversion** systematically distorts everyday spending choices.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
loss (mất mát) + aversion (ác cảm, né tránh) → con người ghét mất mát hơn là thích được lợi tương đương.
vocabulary.common_error: Không nhầm 'loss aversion' (thiên kiến tâm lý về mất mát, thuật ngữ của Kahneman & Tversky) với 'risk aversion' (né tránh rủi ro nói chung) — hai khái niệm liên quan nhưng không đồng nhất.
vocabulary.definition_en: the psychological tendency to feel the pain of a loss more strongly than the pleasure of an equivalent gain
vocabulary.definition_vi: tâm lý sợ mất mát (cảm giác mất mát tác động mạnh hơn cảm giác đạt được tương đương)
vocabulary.example: What contemporary behavioural economics demonstrates is that loss aversion systematically distorts everyday spending choices.
vocabulary.memory_hook: loss (mất mát) + aversion (ác cảm, né tránh) → con người ghét mất mát hơn là thích được lợi tương đương.
